newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns citizens against travel to Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns citizens against travel to Sierra Leone.

text.p: The United States has urged its citizens in Sierra Leone to stay indoors and is prepared to evacuate them if necessary following a coup in the West African country, a White House spokesman said on Sunday.
The spokesman, Barry Toiv, also said the U.S. embassy there had been hit twice by rocket-propelled grenades but that no one was hurt.
Soldiers in Sierra Leone ousted the civilian government on Sunday and President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah flew into exile in Guinea.

Coup leaders announced a dusk-to-dawn curfew and warned Nigerian peacekeeping troops in the capitol of Freetown not to intervene. Residents reported gunfire and looting by uniformed men hours after the coup spokesman called for calm.

"We have advised U.S. citizens in Sierra Leone to stay indoors and we've made preparations, in the event that there needs to be an evacuation, but there is no evacuation going on at this point," Toiv said.
"We are obviously concerned not only about the threat to civilians but also the threat to democracy in Sierra Leone," Toiv added.
The State Department issued a public announcement later on Sunday telling U.S. citizens to defer all travel to Sierra Leone, calling the situation there "extremely dangerous."
Americans in Freetown had been advised by the U.S. embassy to "stand fast wherever they are currently located" and the same guideline was in effect for Americans in other cities.
The State Department also urged all U.S. citizens to listen to Voice of America broadcasts for further updates.

In Sierra Leone, a sergeant who identified himself as one of the coup leaders told Reuters that the army had seized parliament and the government offices at State House, as well as the radio and television.
Heavy gunfire broke out soon after 5 a.m. from the direction of State House and the military headquarters, with troops using machine guns, mortars and rocket-propelled grenades.
